book_title: Chapter 3: Inside the Rajkot Factory, Distribution Reach & Unit Economics
question: How does Macpower manufacture, distribute, and service its machines—and what does every ₹100 of revenue yield in profit and cash?

epigraph.quote: In precision manufacturing, you win the first order with the machine's price, and you win the next ten with the service engineer's response time.
epigraph.author: Machine Tool Distribution Principle

web_blocks.html: Macpower's go-to-market model blends direct technical sales with selective dealers for standard machines [11, 14, 15]. As of Q2 FY27, the company covers 39 Indian cities through 9 branch offices and 9 technology centers [4, 15]. Four more tech centers in Kolhapur, Mumbai, Chennai, and Aurangabad are set to open in Q3 FY27, backed by over 995 employees [4, 15]. Direct sales engineers handle custom NEXA machines, large accounts (Hero, Kirloskar, Graphite India), and government or defence tenders [11, 15]. Dealers stock fast-moving catalog lathes on 30–60 day credit for MSMEs that need quick delivery [11, 15]. Management plans to double its sales and service team by late FY27 ahead of the 13-acre plant launch [4, 15].

Manufacturing runs at the 8-acre Metoda GIDC site in Rajkot. In November 2025, a 40,000 sq ft rented unit lifted annual capacity from 2,000 to 2,500 machines [9, 15]. Backward integration drives Macpower's cost edge. The firm makes 40%–45% of its component count in-house, including sheet-metal covers, powder coating, control panels, and 1,700–1,800 spindles per year [6, 15]. Key precision parts—ball screws, linear guideways, bearings, and CNC controllers (FANUC, Siemens, Mitsubishi)—are still imported. Those imports drove ₹24.14 Cr of forex outgo in FY26 [2, 6, 15]. Management aims to lift in-house component share to 75%–80% once the 60-acre backward-integration site is built [6, 7].

Payment terms vary sharply by sales channel. MSME buyers pay an advance at booking and settle the balance upon bank-loan payout [15]. In H1 FY27, Macpower tightened credit by stopping dispatches against third-party finance assurance letters. That shift cut receivables from ₹46.27 Cr in March 2026 to ₹22.89 Cr in September 2026 [15, 16]. Large corporates pay 80%–90% before dispatch and 10%–20% after installation [10, 15]. Government and defence tenders carry 90-day post-commissioning terms, and March inspection cutoffs often push Q4 revenue into Q1 [10, 11, 15].

web_blocks.caption: Macpower CNC: FY26 Unit Economics Waterfall — Per ₹100 of Revenue (Mar 2026 Standalone)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every ₹100 of FY26 sales, Macpower earned ₹16.22 in EBITDA and ₹10.21 in Net Profit, but converted only ₹4.20 into Operating Cash Flow and ₹0.90 into Free Cash Flow because ₹145.6 Cr of component and WIP inventory absorbed working capital [1, 15].

web_blocks.html: The waterfall highlights the core tension in Macpower's business model. On the income statement, unit economics look strong: a ~38% gross margin (62% raw material cost) and ~3x–5x asset turnover potential [1, 15]. With tiny interest costs, the firm earns a 10.2% net margin and 29% ROCE [1, 15]. On the cash-flow statement, stocking 20,000+ part types and a year-long buffer of imported controllers and ball screws ties up cash [1, 7]. As a result, FY26 Free Cash Flow was just ₹3 Cr despite ₹34 Cr of Net Profit [1].

Analysts must also account for steep quarterly seasonality and fixed-cost leverage. Historically, Q1 brings only 15%–20% of annual sales as MSMEs pause after March budgets and April–May bank lending slows [6, 10]. Q2 and Q3 each bring 20%–25%, while Q4 delivers 30%–35% of annual revenue [6, 10]. Because ~90% of non-material costs—plant overhead, branch rents, and salaried staff—are fixed, EBITDA margins swing widely with quarterly volume [15, 17]. Recent list-price hikes (enacted 2–3 months before October 2026) are only starting to reach Q3 FY27 billing as older backlog clears [15].

web_blocks.title: Operating Leverage & Pricing Lag Mechanics
paragraphs: In Q2 FY27, employee costs rose 25% YoY to ₹11.58 Cr while sales jumped 40.4% to ₹120.33 Cr, showing strong fixed-cost absorption [15]. Even so, EBITDA margin stayed flat at 16.6% (vs 16.5% YoY) because other expenses rose 58% to ₹14.62 Cr on new branches, trade shows, and sales hiring [15].
Because Q2 FY27 dispatches came from older order-book pricing and existing stock, recent price hikes should start lifting gross margins from Q3 FY27 onward [15].

book_paragraphs: If you want to know why a small-town job shop in Ludhiana or Coimbatore buys a Macpower machine instead of a cheaper unbranded lathe, the answer is not just the sticker price. It is what happens on a Tuesday afternoon six months later when a spindle alarm stops production. In the machine-tool business, downtime costs a factory owner far more than a 5% discount on purchase price. That is why Macpower has spent two decades building a physical footprint across 39 Indian cities—9 branch offices and 9 technology centers, with four more opening in Kolhapur, Mumbai, Chennai, and Aurangabad—where customers can test-cut parts before buying and summon a service engineer quickly afterward.

Behind that sales and service web sits a two-tier supply chain in Rajkot that explains both Macpower's high margins and its heavy inventory. Inside its 8-acre Metoda plant, Macpower makes roughly 40% to 45% of its component count itself: sheet-metal enclosures, powder coating, electrical panels, and about 1,700 to 1,800 spindles a year. Making those parts in-house is why Macpower's operating margin is 16% instead of 8%. At the same time, Rupesh Mehta is realistic about what not to make. Just as carmakers do not manufacture their own tires, Macpower buys ball screws, linear guideways, bearings, and CNC controllers from global specialists like FANUC, Siemens, and Mitsubishi—spending ₹24.14 crore in foreign exchange in FY26 alone.

Now let us trace what happens to every ₹100 of revenue that walks through Macpower's door in FY26. Out of ₹333 crore in total sales—roughly 1,666 machines at an average price of ₹20 lakh—₹83.78 per ₹100 goes to raw materials, employee salaries, and branch expenses, leaving ₹16.22 in operating profit. Subtract ₹2.10 for depreciation and just ₹0.60 for interest, and Macpower earns ₹13.51 before tax and ₹10.21 in net profit after tax. For a capital-goods manufacturer, a 10.2% net margin with virtually zero debt is enviable.

But keep your eyes on the bottom of that waterfall, because this is where amateur investors get fooled. Out of ₹10.21 in net profit per ₹100 of sales, only ₹4.20 actually arrived as operating cash flow in FY26, and after ₹3.30 of capital expenditure, just ₹0.90 was left as free cash flow. Where did the rest of the cash go? Straight onto the warehouse shelves. To keep 388 machine models flowing without waiting six months for imported German or Japanese parts, Macpower holds 20,000 different part types—locking up ₹145.6 crore in inventory at March 2026.

The encouraging news is that management proved in the first half of FY27 that it can tighten the tap when it chooses to. By refusing to ship machines on third-party finance assurance letters and waiting for real cash, Macpower cut receivables in half and generated nearly ₹30 crore of operating cash flow in just six months. Still, you and I should remember the trade-off: high-mix CNC manufacturing is inherently inventory-hungry.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice the gap between ₹10.21 of Net Profit and ₹0.90 of Free Cash Flow per ₹100 of FY26 sales. In a fast-growing machine-tool company, growth eats cash before it spits cash out. The real test of Macpower's unit economics is whether H1 FY27's cash-conversion discipline holds once the 13-acre plant comes online.
